content: A dangerous good refers to any solid, liquid, or gas that poses a risk to human health, other living organisms, property, or the environment. In the United States, the term hazardous material (hazmat) is commonly used as an equivalent. Dangerous goods can exhibit various hazardous properties, such as being radioactive, flammable, explosive, toxic, corrosive, biohazardous, oxidizing, asphyxiating, pathogenic, or allergenic. These materials may also have other characteristics that make them dangerous under specific conditions. To mitigate the risks associated with hazardous materials, safety precautions are often necessary during their transportation, use, storage, and disposal. Most countries have legal regulations governing hazardous materials, and these are often aligned with international treaties. Individuals who handle dangerous goods are typically required to wear protective equipment. Additionally, many metropolitan fire departments maintain specialized response teams trained to manage accidents and spills involving hazardous materials. These teams often undergo training at specialized institutions, such as the California Specialized Training Institute, the Texas A&M TEEX Academy, Signet North America, the Justice Institute of British Columbia, and the U.S. National Fire Academy. Laws and regulations regarding the use and handling of hazardous materials can vary depending on the activity and the material's status. For instance, different requirements may apply to workplace use, spill response, consumer sales, or transportation. The transportation of dangerous goods is one of the most widely regulated aspects of hazardous materials management. The United Nations Economic and Social Council's Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods issues Model Regulations, which serve as a framework for many regional and national regulatory systems. For example, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has developed air transport regulations based on the UN Model, with modifications for the unique requirements of air travel. These are further refined by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) to produce the widely used IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations. Similarly, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has created the IMO Dangerous Goods Regulations for maritime transport. Many countries have harmonized their national regulations with the UN Model, both in terms of structure and specific requirements. Dangerous goods are categorized into classes based on their chemical properties and associated risks. The labeling and safety marks for these goods are derived from the UN-based system, but not all countries use identical graphics or text. Some nations use symbols without English wording or adapt the wording to their national language. For accurate information, it is essential to refer to the specific Dangerous Goods Transportation Regulations of the relevant country. In Australia, the standard international UN numbers are used, with some minor variations in vehicle signage. The country also employs the HAZCHEM code, similar to the system used in the United Kingdom, to provide emergency services with advisory information during incidents. In Canada, the transportation of dangerous goods by road is generally under provincial jurisdiction, while air, marine, and rail transport fall under federal authority. The federal government has established the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and regulations, which most provinces have adopted, either fully or partially, through their own legislation. Transport Canada coordinated the creation of these federal regulations, which align with the UN Model. Minor provincial variations may exist, but the federal regulations serve as the standard across the country. In Europe, the European Union has implemented numerous directives and regulations to control hazardous substances, including the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Directive and the REACH regulation. Long-standing treaties, such as ADR (for road transport) and RID (for rail transport), regulate the movement of hazardous materials across European countries, following the guidance of the UN Model. In the United States, concerns about terrorism in the early 21st century led to increased funding for HAZMAT-handling capabilities, recognizing that flammable, toxic, explosive, or radioactive substances could be exploited as weapons. The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) regulates the transportation of hazardous materials under Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations (49 CFR). The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) oversees workplace handling and response to hazardous materials incidents, primarily through the HAZWOPER (Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response) regulations found in 29 CFR 1910.120. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulates hazardous materials to protect communities and the environment, including rules for environmental cleanup and waste disposal. The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) oversees hazardous materials in consumer products. The DOT classifies hazardous materials into nine classes, some of which are further divided into divisions, based on the UN Model. Materials in transportation must be appropriately labeled, packaged, and placarded. Some materials always require placards, while others may only need them under specific conditions. Trailers carrying hazardous goods are typically marked with a four-digit UN number, which first responders can reference in the Emergency Response Guidebook to obtain information about the material. For fixed facilities, different standards apply to the handling and marking of hazardous materials. These include the NFPA 704 diamond markings (a consensus standard often adopted by local governments), OSHA regulations requiring chemical safety information for employees, and CPSC requirements for public labeling. Workers handling hazardous materials in such facilities may also need to wear hazmat suits for protection.
